title: Closures
intro: Closures are anonymous functions written `|args| body`. They can use variables from around them.

coming_from.go: `|x: i32| x * factor` is `func(x int) int { return x * factor }`, usually with the types left out. A closure that changes a captured variable must itself be `let mut`, and `move` makes it take ownership of what it uses.
coming_from.kotlin: `|x| x * factor` is `{ x: Int -> x * factor }`. A closure that changes a captured variable must be stored in a `let mut`, and while it's still going to be used, you can't read that variable yourself.
coming_from.python: A closure is a `lambda` that can hold a whole block with `|| { ... }`. Python makes you say `nonlocal` to change a captured variable; Rust makes you say `mut`: the closure itself must be `let mut`.
coming_from.typescript: `|x| x * factor` is the arrow function `(x) => x * factor`. A closure that changes a captured variable must be `let mut`, and while it's still going to be used, nothing else can read or write that variable.
coming_from.java: `|x| x * factor` is a lambda, but Rust closures may change captured locals. Java forbids that; the workaround is an `AtomicInteger`, a one-element array or a field. A closure that changes something must itself be declared `let mut`.
coming_from.csharp: `|x| x * factor` is a lambda like `x => x * factor`, and like C# it can change captured variables. Rust adds two rules: a closure that changes state must be `let mut`, and while it holds that borrow nobody else can use `count`.
coming_from.c: C has no closures; you'd pass a function pointer plus a `void *` for context. A Rust closure bundles both, captures variables by itself, and is type-checked, so there's no cast from `void *`.
coming_from.cpp: A closure is a lambda that works out its own capture list: it borrows what it reads, borrows mutably what it changes, and `move` takes ownership. Rust needs `let mut` for a closure that changes what it captured even when it changes it through a reference, where a C++ `[&]` lambda needs nothing.

notes: A closure borrows what it uses. `times` holds a `&factor`, and `inc` holds a `&mut count`.
While `inc` is still going to be used, nothing else can touch `count`. That is the one-writer rule. Reading `count` works here because `inc` is never used again after that line.

`move |x| ...` makes the closure take ownership of what it uses instead of borrowing. A closure given to `thread::spawn` needs it when it uses local variables, because the thread can outlive the function that started it (see Threads).
Rust works out from the body whether a closure is `Fn` (only reads), `FnMut` (changes something) or `FnOnce` (gives something away). A function that takes a closure says which kind it accepts.

gotcha.title: A changing closure without mut
gotcha.looks_fine: Go and Kotlin closures can change captured variables freely.
gotcha.rust_sees: `inc` carries a hidden `&mut count` inside it. Calling `inc` changes something, so `inc` itself counts as a value that changes.
gotcha.why: It is the same rule as in Methods: anything that changes has to be marked `mut`, so you can spot every place where state changes.

go.says: Go runs this and prints count=2. Any closure can change the variables it captured, with nothing to mark.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints count=2. A lambda stored in a `val` can still change a captured `var`.

python.says: Python raises UnboundLocalError. Assigning to `count` inside `inc` makes it a new local variable, so you need `global count` (or `nonlocal` in a nested function).
python.code:
count = 0


def inc():
    count += 1


inc()
inc()
print(f"count={count}")

    ^^^^^

typescript.says: Prints count=2. A TypeScript arrow function can change outer `let` variables with no extra marking.

java.says: Java refuses this too, for a different reason: a lambda can't change a local variable it captures. Use an AtomicInteger or a field instead.

csharp.says: C# lambdas can change captured variables with no extra marker, so this prints count=2.

c.says: C has no closures. A function that changes a counter takes a pointer to it, as in the lesson.

cpp.says: A `[&]` lambda can change `count` without any marker, so this prints `count=2`. Capture by value and C++ also wants a keyword: `mutable`.

python.code:
factor = 3
times = lambda x: x * factor  # reads factor

    global count  # needed to change a variable from outside
    count += 1


inc()
inc()
print(f"count={count}")
